chapter: Learning from players; Jonah Jones lessons
title: Ben Webster's hip language and Cab's dictionary
summary: Webster collected slang, and Cab picked it up for his dictionary.

story.theme_name: How I got my name: nicknames and band monikers
story.community_name: How I got my name: nicknames and band names

blocks.x: Did you ever know the sort of thing that Ben talked about, like he had a language all his own.
Oh, yeah. I memorized some of them. He would pick these things up, he said he overheard this couple in the next room, a guy seducing a girl, and he loved these lines.
She said, baby, he says, you beat my line and you beat my wind. Kill me daddy, but don't hurt yourself. You beat my line and you beat my wind. What a wonderful way to put it, you know.
St. Louis, is that where he's from?
But his mother taught school there. I can't say it was his language, but he knew more of it than anybody I know.

He collected it and he could use it. And Cab Calloway, in Cab Calloway's band, Cab Calloway was an exponent of the hipsters, and Cab, quiet as it's kept, picked up a lot of this stuff from Ben, which became Cab's dictionary*, but really these were Ben's line. Like a chick was a soft, a white guy was a gray. And $100.00 was a cow.
And two hours was a deuce of chimes.
I just got this new vine and it cost me a cow and a calf.
I'd forgotten about that. You just
reminded me. I had memorized some of that.
A lame is a dumb cat.
I know, but I wonder where the word came from. Earle Warren uses that all of the time.
Yeah, he's the guy that hangs around, the kind that asks 'you where you're going from here'. This lady, for that was and Chu Berry's answer / 'straight up.' (Laughter.)
